tracks.title: A login screen drawn over a leak
tracks.text: Lesson one point seven — postures. A sub-lesson, under the workbooks lesson… the one about the unit itself. And it starts with a collision. The parent lesson pitched the whole idea in one move — the file carries everything, hand it to anyone. Then your workbook grows a paid dataset… or a client's numbers… and the pitch flips into a threat. If the data rides in the file, anyone with the file has the data. The industry's reflex is to draw a login screen over it. You have seen this artifact a hundred times — the protected HTML export… the password prompt in JavaScript… the dashboard that politely hides its numbers. [sighs] And you know how it ends. View source defeats the lock. The gate and the secret traveled in the same file, and a guard that ships alongside the treasure guards nothing. So the question this lesson answers — how does a single-file format do security that is not theater? The short version, up front. Security is not a property you bolt onto the file. It is a stance you declare… and the stance decides where the bytes are allowed to live at all.

tracks.title: A stance, not a feature
tracks.text: A stance, not a feature — the definition. A posture is a declared security stance on a workbook — public… gated data… or gated route — and it decides which bytes may be baked into a static artifact, and which may only ever exist behind the runtime, released per-request, after auth. The set is exactly three, and each answers one question. What is public — everything, the shell, or nothing? First… public. Fully public. The whole workbook may be rendered into one static HTML file — no secrets, openable anywhere, forever. Second… gated data. The shell is public — but the data and the capabilities are fetched from the runtime, per request, behind auth. The app behind the page is the runtime… not the file. Third… gated route. Even the shell — even the workbook's existence — is private. The runtime serves it only to an authenticated caller. There is a canon table for this, and its verdict fits in one sentence — only the public posture is safe on a static host… both gated postures say no. And declaring one is a single line of metadata — a posture key on the workbook, or publish access in the publish file. The parser is forgiving about dashes and casing… an empty value parses to public… but an unknown string is an error, not a guess. [chuckles] A security stance is the one place a parser should refuse to be creative.

tracks.title: The anti-leak rule
tracks.text: Next — the anti-leak rule. Everything in this lesson hangs off one law, stated in the access module's own documentation. A gated workbook must never be rendered into a public static artifact… because a static file ships its contents to anyone with the URL. Client-side gating is theater. The secret cannot be guarded inside the artifact — it has to never enter the artifact. The primitive carrying the law is one tiny function… static safe. True for public. False for both gated postures. Picture the fork it creates. The workbook's posture flows in, and the function asks one question. If the answer is true — public — the whole workbook bakes into one static HTML file, and that is fine, because there are no secrets to leak. If the answer is false — either gated posture — the bytes are never inlined. They stay behind the runtime, released per request, after auth. [curious] Read that second branch carefully, because it is the whole design. It does not say… inlined behind a password. It says the bytes do not go into the file. There is no version of a gated workbook whose secrets sit in a static artifact waiting for a cleverer attacker. The artifact that exists just does not contain them. And one deliberate nuance. Even the desktop app — running on a machine you trust — gets only a shell for gated workbooks, fetching the protected content over the runtime connection. Not because your laptop is the enemy… but because a desktop artifact is still a file, and files get copied to web hosts. The invariant does not trust contexts. It trusts construction.

tracks.title: Enforced twice, at build time
tracks.text: Enforced twice — at build time. An invariant that lives only in request handlers is a hope. This one is enforced where you cannot route around it… in the pipeline that produces artifacts, at two separate guards. Guard one — the publish validator. There are four publish targets. Cloudflare pages… github pages… self-hosted… and desktop app. The first two are public static hosts, and the validator flatly rejects a gated posture aimed at either. Here is the worked example. A publish file for a fictional gated workbook — target, cloudflare pages… project, acme pricing… access, gated data. Run publish validate, and it fails with an error worth hearing verbatim. Gated data cannot publish to cloudflare pages — a public static host ships the whole workbook to anyone… client-side gating is theater. Use self-hosted, where the runtime gates per request… or desktop app, a local shell. Flip the target to self-hosted, and validation passes. [excited] The invariant is a build error, not a runtime hope. You cannot ship the leak, because the pipeline will not produce the file. And the refusal is pinned by the test suite — error string and all. Guard two — the compiler. The desktop app target accepts gated workbooks… but its compiler branches on that same static safe question. Public posture — the rendered page is inlined, plus a runtime bootstrap. Gated posture — it emits a gated shell. A generated public page with no workbook content inside… whose entire body says, this workbook is protected, please sign in… and which fetches the real content from the runtime only after auth. The source comment gives the reason in one line. Even a desktop artifact can be copied to a web host. Open that shell once and view its source — a loading message, a sign-in prompt, a fetch… and not one byte of the workbook. The thing the attacker downloads is honestly empty.

tracks.title: The twelve-line judge
tracks.text: Now a depth rung — the twelve-line judge. At request time the posture meets a tiny total function. Enforce takes three arguments — the posture… the demand… and the identity — and returns allow, or deny, auth required. The demand vocabulary has three words. Shell — the app and its structure. Data — the protected content and capabilities. And full — both, inlined. The whole decision is a small matrix, and here it is, spoken. Public allows everything, for anyone — even anonymous. Gated data allows the shell for anyone… but data and full require an authenticated identity. Gated route requires authentication for everything — even the shell. And authenticated is strict. The identity must carry a real user id — not missing, not empty… and not the word dev. The anonymous developer fallback explicitly does not count. The test suite says it in six lines, and two of them matter most. Enforce, gated data, data, with a real user — allow. Enforce, gated data, data, with the dev identity — deny. [curious] That dev line is the trap worth memorizing. Local development cannot fake its way past a gate… so it worked on my machine can never quietly mean the gate was open on my machine. If gating appears to work in dev, it is because you presented a real identity — not because the judge went easy on you.

tracks.title: Five rungs to an identity
tracks.text: Five rungs to an identity. The judge needs an identity to judge… and identities come out of the auth ladder — five rungs, checked top to bottom, first match wins. First — the public allowlist. The health endpoint and the well-known discovery documents are always open, for a bootstrap reason the source spells out. A client must be able to read the capabilities document to learn which rung it needs… before it has any credential. The handshake even advertises the rung — o-i-d-c j-w-t on a multi-tenant deploy, trusted otherwise. Second — the desktop per-boot token. Twenty-four random bytes… minted fresh every boot… compared in constant time… scoping to the local tenant. It reaches the desktop shell through a discovery file readable only by you — possession of the local file is the credential, and it expires with the process. Third — the shared-secret lock. Set the public bearer variable and the deploy is locked. The exact secret maps to the configured tenant… and any other or absent bearer is a four-oh-one — with no dev fallback. One secret, one tenant, nothing anonymous. Fourth — the JWT rung. Production multi-tenant… tokens issued by the auth service, verified against published keys, carrying the user, the organization as tenant, and the session — and living one hour. With no bearer at all on a multi-tenant deploy, the answer is tenant required… because isolation cannot rest on a spoofable header. And fifth — the dev fallback, only when the deploy is neither locked nor multi-tenant. A tenant header, or just the word dev, becomes the tenant. But notice the shape it produces — a user id of dev… which is exactly the identity the judge refuses. [chuckles] The bottom rung gets you in the door for development. It never gets you through a gate. One more thing every rung shares — the deny. One uniform error envelope, a closed vocabulary of seven codes… so a refusal never becomes an information channel.

tracks.title: Watch the gate hold
tracks.text: Watch the gate hold — the key release, live, end to end. The clearest place to see posture, judge, and ladder working together is the sealed bundle. The bundles lesson taught the cipher layer — a sealed entry ships as real ciphertext, one fresh key per entry, and the key never rides in the bundle. It sits in an escrow table at the runtime, keyed by workbook id and entry path. This lesson owns the other layer… who gets the key, and when. Follow one request through. A client holding the sealed bundle posts to the key release endpoint, naming the key id. The runtime asks the judge exactly one question — enforce, gated data, data, with this identity. If the identity is real… the judge allows, the runtime fetches the thirty-two byte key from escrow, and returns it with the algorithm name. If the caller is anonymous — or dev — the judge denies… and the client gets a four-oh-one. Two curl commands tell the whole story. The anonymous one comes back with the error envelope — code unauthorized, not retryable. The authenticated one — say, a locked deploy presenting its shared secret — comes back with the key id, the algorithm, a-e-s two fifty-six g-c-m… and the key itself, base sixty-four. And here is the subtle part. [whispers] The anonymous refusal is byte-identical to any unauthorized call on the runtime — whether the key exists, does not exist, or never did. Fail closed… no oracle. A probing client learns nothing from being refused. Only after auth does a missing key become an honest four-oh-four — because at that point you have earned a real answer. Revocation is a delete from the escrow table, one entry at a time. The source calls this design a dead-man switch, and names what it is not. Not obfuscation… not a forked format… not a client-side guard — all bypassable, because the attacker owns the client and the bytes. The real gate is a key the client lacks.

tracks.title: Which posture is yours
tracks.text: So — which posture is yours? The rubric is shorter than the theory. Ask one question. What must stay private — nothing, the data, or the existence? If sharing with anyone is the point — a demo, a report, a brand book — that is public, and it can publish anywhere, static hosts included. If you want a free shell over paid or private data — try the app, authenticate for the numbers — that is gated data… and it publishes to self-hosted or the desktop app, never to a static host. And if even the existence of the tool is private — an internal app — that is gated route, same two doors. Now the price tag, stated plainly. A gated workbook needs a reachable runtime. The hand-it-to-anyone story still applies to the shell — a gated data shell is a real public page — but the gated parts go inert without an engine answering per request. That is not a limitation snuck in beside the feature. It is the feature. The only way the file cannot leak the secret… is if the file does not have the secret. And then something else must. One contrast to keep the vocabulary clean. A posture answers who may read this. Provenance — who made it, whether it has been touched — is a different question with a different mechanism… the signatures story. A workbook can be public and signed, or gated and unsigned. The two axes do not trade.

tracks.title: Why the default is public
tracks.text: A depth rung — why the default is public. Look up the posture of a workbook that never declared one… and you get public. [curious] Every security instinct you have just flinched. Fail open is wrong — defaults should deny. The module's own documentation makes the counter-argument, and it is worth making rather than hiding. An unregistered workbook carries no server-side secrets to leak. It is its static self — everything it has is already in the file, which is the parent lesson's whole deal. There is nothing behind the runtime to protect… because nothing was ever put behind the runtime. A workbook becomes gated the only way it can mean anything — by explicitly declaring it. And at that moment, the invariant takes over and the static paths slam shut. Fail open would be wrong if the default could expose something. It cannot — declaring the posture and possessing the secret arrive together. And there is a belt-and-braces guard for the mistake the default cannot cover… a secret pasted into the publish file itself. The validator sniffs for it. Property keys ending in token, key, secret, account, password, or credential… and values that look like long hex strings… draw a warning — use an environment variable instead. The posture system keeps secrets out of artifacts. The warnings keep them out of the config that travels with the project.

tracks.title: Where the wiring ends
tracks.text: Now the honest part — where the wiring ends. Four edges, stated plainly. First… the per-route registry is a follow-on. The judge exists, is tested, and is live where it matters most — the key release and the publish pipeline both call it. But wiring every serving route to a per-workbook posture registry needs the metadata to carry the posture everywhere… and that wiring is still in progress. The contract and the primitive are real. Universal coverage is not, yet. Second… gated route is the least-wired stance. Its contract is exact — even the shell requires auth, and the judge enforces it in one line — but of the three postures it has the least end-to-end serving path behind it today. Treat it as a declared contract with an enforcement primitive… not a finished feature. Third… a locked deploy is a shared secret, not identities. The public bearer gives you one credential for one tenant — everyone holding it is the same caller. And as the auth cascade reads, a locked deploy accepts the shared secret, not JWTs — lock mode and per-user JWT mode are different deploys, not layers of one. If you need to know which user opened the gate, you need the JWT rung. And fourth… gating binds you to a runtime. Said once more, because it is the honest cost. Public workbooks are open anywhere, forever. Gated ones are alive exactly as long as a runtime answers for them. [sighs] Real gates need a gatekeeper with a power supply.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Can I just hide the data with JavaScript? You can write the code, but it is not a gate — the data and the check ship in the same file, and view source reads both. The system's word for this is theater… and it refuses to participate. Aim a gated posture at a static host, and the validator fails the build before the leaking artifact exists. What does someone holding my gated bundle actually have? Ciphertext, and key references. The manifest names which key unlocks which entry — never the key itself. The useful thing they hold is an invitation to authenticate. Does a tenant header in dev unlock gated data? No. The dev fallback produces the one identity the judge explicitly rejects… and the test suite pins it. Can I change a posture later? Yes — it is a declaration, one metadata line, re-read on the next build and the next request. One arrow of time, though. Bytes already published into static artifacts were public when they left… and no declaration recalls them. And — what is the difference between a posture and a sealed entry? Stance versus mechanism. The posture is the declared decision — who may read what, where bytes may live. The seal is one enforcement mechanism under it — ciphertext in the artifact, key in escrow, released only when the judge allows. The posture decides. The seal carries the decision into the bytes.

tracks.title: Back up to the parent
tracks.text: So that is postures. Three stances — public… gated data… gated route. One law — gated bytes never enter a static artifact, enforced as a build error at two guards. One twelve-line judge, fed by a five-rung ladder… and one live gate, where the only thing standing between an attacker and the data is a key the client lacks. [chuckles] Which is the only kind of standing that counts. The way back up is short. This sits under lesson one — the workbook itself, the unit and its promise. And the closest sibling is bundles — the carton, and the cipher layer this lesson's gate sits on top of. The file carries everything it is allowed to carry… and not one byte more. That is the posture.
